text: Questions nine and ten. What is the population stability index? And how do you detect drift when labels are delayed or unavailable? PSI compares one feature's distribution now with its distribution in training. Cut the training values into ten buckets of equal share, then add up, over the buckets, the difference in share times the log of their ratio. In a simulation, a slight shift scores point oh one, and a large one, one point four. Under point one is called stable, and over point two needs action, but those are conventions, not significance tests. With labels late, PSI or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on each input, and on the predictions, is your early warning. It can show that something moved; it can't prove the model got worse. For that, measure outcomes: delayed labels, audits, or a small randomized slice. Calibrate the threshold to your traffic, because PSI is noisy on small samples. With no drift at all, a window of a hundred values scores over point one almost half the time. A window of a thousand: never, in two thousand tries. And leave the outer buckets open. Edges cut at the training minimum and maximum drop anything beyond them from the count. Simulate a fifth of values arriving past anything seen in training: closed edges read point oh three, stable. Open ones read point two five.
